title: Data Visualization with Tableau
tagline: Build charts the Tableau way in a live viz builder in your browser: shelves, marks, calculated fields, table calculations and LOD expressions
summary: Learn visual analytics the way Tableau teaches it: fields on shelves, the Marks card, filters, calculated fields, table calculations and level-of-detail expressions, then design, dashboards, data preparation, performance and publishing. A live viz builder in your browser has the same shelves and writes real Tableau calculation syntax, so you build and check the charts yourself. Tableau Desktop is a desktop application and does not run in a browser, so dashboards, actions, Prep, publishing and security are explained with scenarios and checked with sorting and writing activities.

modules.title: Tableau basics: fields, shelves and your first charts
modules.summary: Learn how Tableau thinks: dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous fields, shelves and the Marks card, and how a chart is built from fields.
modules.outcome: You can tell dimensions from measures and discrete from continuous, say what the Columns, Rows and Marks shelves do, and build a bar chart, a horizontal bar chart and a sorted view.
modules.intro: Tableau is the best-known tool for visual analysis, and its big idea is simple: you do not choose a chart type and then feed it data. You put fields on shelves, and Tableau draws the chart that fits. Learn what the shelves mean and you can build almost any chart. This module teaches that grammar. A practice viz builder runs in your browser with the same shelves, so you build the charts yourself. Tableau Desktop and Tableau Public are desktop applications and do not run in a browser tab, so the steps described here (opening Tableau, connecting, publishing) are explained rather than run. What does run here is a practice viz builder with the same ideas: fields on the Columns and Rows shelves, the Marks card, filters, calculated fields and table calculations, on a real table.

topics.title: What Tableau is, and its products
topics.html:
Tableau is a visual analytics platform: you connect to data, drag fields onto a canvas, and Tableau turns them into charts, dashboards and stories that people can explore.

The Tableau family
ProductWhat it isTypical use
Tableau DesktopA paid desktop application (Windows and Mac)Connect to data, build and publish visualisations
Tableau PublicA free desktop application, with a public galleryLearning, portfolios and public data. Work is saved publicly
Tableau Prep BuilderA data preparation toolClean, combine and reshape data before analysis
Tableau Cloud and Tableau ServerOnline and self-hosted serversPublish, share and secure workbooks and data sources for an organisation
Tableau MobileApps for phones and tabletsView and interact with dashboards
Definition

Workbook, sheet, dashboard, story. A workbook is the file. A sheet is one view (one chart or table). A dashboard arranges several sheets on one page with filters and actions. A story is a sequence of sheets or dashboards that leads a reader through a narrative.

Worked example

A small team's use

A distributor's analyst builds a sales dashboard.

  1. She connects Tableau Desktop to the company database and builds three sheets: sales by region, monthly trend, and profit by sub-category.
  2. She combines them into a dashboard with a region filter.
  3. She publishes it to Tableau Cloud, where managers open it in a browser and on their phones.

Answer. Sheets are the building blocks; the dashboard is what people use.

Watch out

Tableau Public publishes your work to the public web. Never use it for private or company data. For internal sharing use Tableau Cloud or Server.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Tableau is only a chart gallery: its strength is exploring data interactively.
  • Using Tableau Public for confidential data.
  • Building everything on one crowded sheet instead of several simple ones.
Try it yourself: What is the difference between a sheet and a dashboard?

Model answer. A sheet is one view; a dashboard arranges several sheets (and filters and actions) on one page.

Check what you just learned

1. Which product is free but publishes your work publicly?
  • Tableau Server
  • Tableau Public (correct)
  • Tableau Prep
  • Tableau Cloud

Tableau Public shares workbooks on the public web.

2. A dashboard is:
  • One chart
  • A data file
  • Several sheets arranged on one page (correct)
  • A colour palette

It combines sheets with filters and actions.
keyPoints: Desktop builds, Public is free but public, Prep cleans data, Cloud and Server share.
A workbook holds sheets, dashboards and stories.
Never use Tableau Public for private data.

topics.title: Dimensions, measures, discrete and continuous
topics.html:
Every field in Tableau's data pane is a dimension or a measure, and every field you use is discrete or continuous. These two ideas explain most of what Tableau does.

Dimensions and measures
DimensionMeasure
What it isA category or label you slice byA number you add up or average
ExamplesRegion, Category, Customer, Order Date, Order IDSales, Profit, Quantity, Discount
What Tableau doesSplits the data into groups, one mark per groupAggregates (sum by default) within each group
In the data paneTop sectionBottom section
Discrete and continuous
Discrete (blue pill)Continuous (green pill)
MeaningSeparate, countable valuesAn unbroken range of values
On a chartAdds headers: one column or row per valueAdds an axis with a scale
Typical fieldsDimensions such as RegionMeasures such as SUM(Sales)
DatesDiscrete: Year, Month as separate labelsContinuous: a smooth timeline

A useful picture: dimensions create the marks, measures give them size. One dimension on Columns and one measure on Rows gives one bar per dimension value, as tall as the measure's total.

Your first chart

Region is a dimension (it makes the bars); SUM(Sales) is a measure (it sets their height). Change Region to Category, or the aggregation to Average, and watch the bars change.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Watch out

Aggregation is the usual surprise. Tableau sums a measure by default. If you put Discount on Rows you get the sum of the discounts, which is meaningless; you almost always want the average. Always check the aggregation in the pill's menu.

Worked example

Choosing the field's role

You drag Order ID onto Columns and get 120 columns.

  1. Order ID is a dimension: it makes one mark per value (one per order).
  2. If you wanted the number of orders, you wanted a measure: COUNTD(Order ID) (distinct count).
  3. Counting the dimension turns it into a measure.

Answer. The same field can be a label or something to count, depending on how you use it.

Common mistakes

  • Putting an identifier such as Order ID on a shelf as a dimension and getting hundreds of marks.
  • Summing a field that should be averaged.
  • Confusing blue and green pills with dimensions and measures: blue and green mean discrete and continuous.
Try it yourself: Which pill colour does SUM(Sales) usually have, and why?

Model answer. Green: it is a continuous measure, so Tableau draws an axis for it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which field is normally a dimension?
  • Sales
  • Profit
  • Quantity
  • Region (correct)

Region is a category you slice by.

2. A green pill on a shelf is:
  • Continuous (correct)
  • Discrete
  • A filter
  • A dimension only

Green means continuous; blue means discrete.
keyPoints: Dimensions group the data into marks; measures are aggregated within each mark.
Discrete (blue) fields add headers; continuous (green) fields add axes.
Check the aggregation of every measure.

topics.title: Shelves and the Marks card
topics.html:
The canvas has a few places to put fields, and each controls one aspect of the chart.

Where a field can go
PlaceWhat it controls
Columns shelfThe horizontal layout: headers or the x-axis
Rows shelfThe vertical layout: headers or the y-axis
Marks card: ColorThe colour of each mark (a dimension gives a legend; a measure gives a colour scale)
Marks card: SizeThe size of each mark
Marks card: LabelText printed on or beside each mark
Marks card: DetailSplits marks into finer groups without changing the look
Marks card: TooltipWhat appears when you hover
Filters shelfWhich rows of data are included

The mark type (bar, line, area, circle, square, text, pie) is also on the Marks card. By default it is Automatic: Tableau picks the mark from the fields you have used.

What Automatic does
You putTableau draws
A dimension on Columns, a measure on RowsVertical bars (a line if the dimension is a date)
A measure on Columns, a dimension on RowsHorizontal bars
A measure on each shelfA scatter plot of circles
A dimension on each shelfA text table (or a heat map with a coloured measure)

Marks, colour and size

Put Category on Color to split the bars into a stack. Try the Marks menu: Circle, Pie, Text. Put Profit on Label.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

Same data, four views

Sales by region.

  1. Region on Columns, SUM(Sales) on Rows: vertical bars.
  2. Swap them: horizontal bars.
  3. Add Category to Color: stacked bars showing the mix inside each region.
  4. Add Profit to Label: the profit printed on each bar.

Answer. Each field on a different shelf changes one thing, which is why you can build a view by adding one field at a time.

Tip

Build a view one field at a time and watch what each addition changes. When a chart looks wrong, remove the last field you added.

Common mistakes

  • Putting a measure on Color when a dimension was meant (a legend of categories needs a dimension).
  • Using Detail when you wanted Color (Detail adds marks without telling them apart).
  • Forgetting to look at the Marks card: the mark type can be set to something other than what you expect.
Try it yourself: Which shelf do you use to split bars into a stack by Category?

Model answer. Color on the Marks card (a dimension on Color stacks the bars).

Check what you just learned

1. Putting a dimension on Color:
  • Does nothing
  • Splits marks by colour and adds a legend (correct)
  • Sorts the chart
  • Deletes marks

Each value gets its own colour.

2. A measure on each of Columns and Rows gives:
  • Bars
  • A pie
  • A scatter plot (correct)
  • A table

Two measures give a position on both axes.
keyPoints: Columns and Rows set the layout; the Marks card sets colour, size, labels and detail.
Automatic marks follow the fields: bars, lines, circles or text.
Add one field at a time and see what changes.

topics.title: Sorting, and bars that read well
topics.html:
A bar chart is the workhorse of business visuals, and a few habits make it read well.

Habits for good bar charts

  • Sort bars by value, largest first, unless the categories have a natural order (months, ratings).
  • Horizontal bars when category names are long.
  • Bars start at zero: Tableau does this by default for bars.
  • Label the value on the bar when exact numbers matter.
  • Limit the number of bars: show the top 10 and group the rest, or filter.

Sort and show the top

Sales by sub-category on horizontal bars. Choose Sort: High to low, then Show: Top 5. Sorting is what makes a bar chart readable.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

Why sorting matters

A bar chart of sales by sub-category is in alphabetical order.

  1. The reader must scan every bar to find the largest.
  2. Sorted high to low, the ranking is obvious in a second.
  3. The best and worst performers sit at the two ends.

Answer. Alphabetical order is rarely the right order. Sort by the measure that matters.

Watch out

Do not sort categories that have a natural order. Months should run January to December, and survey ratings from low to high; sorting them by value scrambles the story.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving bars in alphabetical order.
  • A vertical bar chart with long, rotated labels.
  • Showing 40 bars when the top 10 tell the story.
Try it yourself: Why use horizontal bars for sub-category names?

Model answer. Long labels read naturally on the left of horizontal bars, where vertical bars would need rotated text.

Check what you just learned

1. When should you NOT sort by value?
  • Never
  • For horizontal bars
  • For long lists
  • When categories have a natural order such as months (correct)

Preserve a natural order.

2. Horizontal bars suit:
  • Long category names (correct)
  • Dates only
  • Pie charts
  • Maps

Labels read left to right.

Key terms: flip and sort

Dimension
A category that groups the data.
Measure
A number that is aggregated.
Discrete
Separate values: blue pills, headers.
Continuous
An unbroken range: green pills, axes.
Shelf
A place to put fields: Columns, Rows, Filters.
Marks card
Controls colour, size, labels, detail and mark type.
Sheet
One view; sheets combine into dashboards.
keyPoints: Sort bars by value unless there is a natural order; use horizontal bars for long names.
Bars start at zero; label values when exact numbers matter.
Show the top N and filter the rest.

modules.title: Core charts: lines, stacks, scatters, heat maps
modules.summary: Build the charts you will use most, choose them by the question, and filter to focus: top N, dimension filters and measure filters.
modules.outcome: You can build line charts with date levels, stacked bars, scatter plots with detail, heat maps and text tables, and filter and rank to focus on what matters.
modules.intro: Five or six chart types cover almost every business question. This module builds each one in the practice viz builder and, more importantly, teaches you which question each one answers. The same fields give different charts depending on where they go, so by the end you should be able to look at a question and know which fields go on which shelves.

topics.title: Lines and trends over time
topics.html:
A line chart shows change over time. Put a date on Columns and a measure on Rows, and Tableau draws a line. The date level (year, quarter, month, day) decides how the time is grouped.

Sales over time

MONTH(Order Date) groups sales by month. Change it to Quarter or Year with the menu on the pill, and add Region to Color for one line per region.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Date levels
LevelGroups the data byUse for
YearCalendar yearLong-run comparison
QuarterYear and quarterBusiness reporting cycles
MonthYear and monthTrends and seasonality
DayEach dateDetailed daily patterns (many marks)
Worked example

Two years, one line per year

You want to compare 2024 and 2025 month by month.

  1. Put MONTH(Order Date) on Columns.
  2. Colour by YEAR(Order Date), so each year has its own line.
  3. The lines overlap month for month and the gap between them is the growth.

Answer. Putting the year on Color rather than in the axis lets you compare the same months across years.

Watch out

A line chart connects points and so implies that the values between them exist. Use lines for continuous time. For separate categories (regions, products) use bars, even when the categories happen to be ordered.

Common mistakes

  • A line chart for unrelated categories.
  • Too many lines (more than five or six) with similar colours.
  • Daily data with hundreds of points when a month would show the trend.
Try it yourself: How do you compare the same months across two years on one chart?

Model answer. Put MONTH(Order Date) on Columns, SUM(Sales) on Rows and YEAR(Order Date) on Color: one line per year.

Check what you just learned

1. A line chart suits:
  • Unrelated categories
  • Change over time (correct)
  • Parts of a whole
  • Rankings of 50 items

Lines show trends.

2. To get one line per year you put YEAR(Order Date) on:
  • Rows
  • Filters only
  • Color (correct)
  • Label

A dimension on Color splits lines.
keyPoints: A date on Columns with a measure on Rows draws a line.
The date level (year, quarter, month, day) sets the grouping.
Compare years by putting the year on Color; keep lines few.

topics.title: Stacks, scatter plots and heat maps
topics.html:
Three more chart types, each answering a different question.

Question to chart
QuestionChartHow to build it
How is each total made up of parts?Stacked barDimension on Columns, measure on Rows, another dimension on Color
Are two measures related? Which items are outliers?Scatter plotA measure on Columns and another on Rows, with a dimension on Detail (one dot per item)
Where are the hot and cold spots across two dimensions?Heat mapA dimension on each shelf, Square mark, a measure on Color

Sales against profit

Each dot is a sub-category (Detail). Dots low on the chart lose money however much they sell. Add Category to Color.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

A heat map of profit

Sub-category down the side, region across the top, colour for profit. Darker means larger. Try a different colour measure.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

Finding the problem with a scatter

You plot Sales (x) against Profit (y), one dot per sub-category.

  1. Most dots rise to the right: more sales, more profit.
  2. Two dots sit well below zero profit despite large sales.
  3. Those sub-categories sell a lot and lose money: the discount policy deserves a look.

Answer. A scatter turns 'which items are unusual?' into a glance.

Watch out

Stacked bars compare only the bottom segment accurately. All other segments start at different heights, so they are hard to compare. If the comparison between parts matters, use side-by-side bars or a heat map instead.

Common mistakes

  • A scatter plot without a Detail field: Tableau sums everything into a single dot.
  • A stacked bar with ten colours.
  • A heat map with a colour scale that is not centred when both gains and losses matter.
Try it yourself: Why does a scatter plot need a dimension on Detail?

Model answer. Without it, Tableau aggregates all rows into one dot; Detail makes one dot per member.

Check what you just learned

1. Which chart shows the relationship between two measures?
  • Pie
  • Text table
  • Stacked bar
  • Scatter plot (correct)

A scatter positions dots by both.

2. A heat map is built with:
  • A dimension on each shelf and a measure on Color (correct)
  • Two measures
  • A date only
  • A map

Rows by columns, coloured by a measure.
keyPoints: Stacked bars show composition; scatter plots show relationships and outliers; heat maps show hot spots.
A scatter needs a Detail dimension for one dot per item.
Stacks compare only the bottom segment well.

topics.title: Filtering and ranking: focus on what matters
topics.html:
Filters decide which data is in the view. The type of field you filter on decides how the filter behaves.

Kinds of filter
FilterWorks onExample
Dimension filterWhich members of a dimension to keepOnly the East and West regions
Measure filterA range of an aggregated measureOnly marks with SUM(Sales) above 10,000
Date filterA range or part of a dateOnly 2025, or the last 3 months
Top NThe N members with the highest (or lowest) measureThe top 10 customers by sales
Context filterA filter that runs first, so others work on its resultTop 5 products within the East region

Filter and rank

Use + Add filter to keep only some regions, or a measure filter on Sales. Then Sort: High to low and Show: Top 5.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

Order matters: Top N and a dimension filter

You want the top 5 customers within the East.

  1. A plain Top 5 customers filter is evaluated over all regions first.
  2. Then the East filter removes some of those five, leaving fewer than five.
  3. Make the Region filter a context filter so it runs first; then Top 5 works within the East.

Answer. Filters run in a fixed order, so the order can change the answer. This is one of the most common Tableau surprises.

Watch out

Show only what the reader needs. A filter that removes rows changes every number in the view, so say what is filtered in the title or a caption ('Technology only, 2025').

Common mistakes

  • Expecting Top N to respect a dimension filter without a context filter.
  • Filtering out data and not saying so.
  • Offering a dozen interactive filters on a dashboard.
Try it yourself: Why make a filter a context filter?

Model answer. So it runs first and other filters, such as Top N, work on its result.

Check what you just learned

1. A context filter:
  • Runs after all others
  • Runs first, so other filters work on its result (correct)
  • Changes colours
  • Sorts data

It sets the data the others work on.

2. A measure filter keeps:
  • Members of a dimension
  • Dates
  • Marks whose aggregated value is in a range (correct)
  • Colours

It filters on the aggregated number.
keyPoints: Dimension, measure, date, Top N and context filters do different jobs.
Filters run in a fixed order; use a context filter so one filter works before another.
Say what is filtered.

topics.title: Choosing the right chart
topics.html:
Choose the chart by the question, not by what is available.

Question to chart
QuestionChart
How much? (compare categories)Bar chart, sorted
How has it changed over time?Line chart
What is it made of?Stacked bar (a pie only for 2 to 4 parts)
Are two things related?Scatter plot
Where are the highs and lows across two categories?Heat map or highlight table
What exactly are the numbers?Text table
How is it distributed?Histogram
Where is it?Map

Questions to ask yourself before you build

  • What is the one question this chart answers?
  • Who is the reader and what will they do with it?
  • Which field is the measure of interest, and which dimensions slice it?
  • Is a table clearer than a chart?
  • What could mislead?
Worked example

Choosing under pressure

A manager asks: 'Are discounts hurting profit?'

  1. The question is about a relationship between two measures: discount and profit.
  2. A scatter of average discount (x) against profit (y), one dot per sub-category, shows it.
  3. A bar chart of each alone would hide the relationship.

Answer. The question names the chart.

Watch out

The default chart from Tableau's Show Me panel is a suggestion, not a verdict. A pie or a map can be technically possible and still a poor choice.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a chart for how it looks.
  • A pie chart for twelve categories.
  • A map when the location is not the point.
Try it yourself: Which chart answers 'which products sell a lot but lose money?'

Model answer. A scatter plot of sales against profit with one dot per product.

Check what you just learned

1. Which chart suits 'how has revenue changed?'
  • Pie
  • Heat map
  • Scatter
  • Line (correct)

Lines show change over time.

2. The best first step in choosing a chart is to:
  • State the question the chart answers (correct)
  • Open Show Me
  • Choose colours
  • Add a legend

The question names the chart.

Key terms: flip and sort

Date level
Year, quarter, month or day.
Stacked bar
Bars split by a second dimension on Color.
Scatter plot
A measure on each axis, one dot per Detail member.
Heat map
A grid coloured by a measure.
Top N
Keep the N highest (or lowest) members.
Context filter
A filter that runs first.
Measure filter
A filter on an aggregated number.
keyPoints: Choose by the question: bars, lines, stacks, scatters, heat maps, tables, histograms, maps.
Decide the one question each chart answers.
Treat Show Me as a suggestion.

modules.title: Calculations: fields, table calcs and LOD expressions
modules.summary: Create calculated fields, use quick table calculations for running totals and percent of total, and control the level of detail with FIXED, INCLUDE and EXCLUDE.
modules.outcome: You can write row-level and aggregate calculated fields, avoid the 'ratio of sums' trap, apply table calculations, and write FIXED, INCLUDE and EXCLUDE expressions.
modules.intro: Tableau's built-in fields rarely answer a real business question on their own. You want a profit ratio, a flag for loss-making orders, a running total, each region's share of its category. This module teaches the three tools for that: calculated fields, table calculations and level-of-detail (LOD) expressions. All three run in the practice viz builder with real Tableau syntax, so you can write them, see them change the chart, and see the errors Tableau would give.

topics.title: Calculated fields: row-level and aggregate
topics.html:
A calculated field is a new field you define with a formula. There are two kinds, and the difference matters.

Row-level and aggregate calculations
Row-levelAggregate
Worked outFor every row of data, then aggregatedOnce per mark, after the rows are grouped
Looks like[Sales] - [Profit]; IF [Profit] < 0 THEN "Loss" ELSE "Profit" ENDSUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])
ResultA new dimension (text) or measure (number)A measure
Use forFlags, bands, per-row arithmeticRatios, averages of totals, percentages
Formula · A ratio, done right

Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])

Divide the totals, not each row's ratio. The result is the correct ratio for every mark, whatever is in the view.

Create a calculated field

Write Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) in the box on the left and press Create field. Then add it to Rows. Try a flag: Result = IF [Profit] < 0 THEN "Loss" ELSE "Profit" END, and put it on Color.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

Why the ratio of sums matters

Two sub-categories have profit ratios of 40% on sales of 100 and 10% on sales of 900.

  1. Average of the two ratios: (40% + 10%) / 2 = 25%.
  2. Ratio of the totals: (40 + 90) / (100 + 900) = 13%.
  3. Most of the sales are at 10%, so the overall ratio must be near 10%.

Answer. SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) gives 13%; averaging the row ratios gives a wrong 25%.

Watch out

You cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate values in one calculation: SUM([Profit]) / [Sales] is an error, because one part is a total and the other a single row. Wrap everything in an aggregate (or use ATTR for a dimension).

Useful functions

  • Logic: IF ... THEN ... ELSEIF ... ELSE ... END, CASE, IIF.
  • Numbers: ROUND, ABS, ZN (null to zero), IFNULL.
  • Text: UPPER, LEFT, CONTAINS, LEN.
  • Dates: YEAR, MONTH, DATETRUNC('month', [Order Date]).
  • Aggregates: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTD, MEDIAN, ATTR.

Common mistakes

  • Averaging row ratios instead of dividing totals.
  • Mixing aggregate and non-aggregate parts.
  • Naming a field the same as an existing one.
Try it yourself: Write the calculated field for the share of sales that comes with a discount, if Discount is 0 when there is none.

Model answer. Row-level flag: IF [Discount] > 0 THEN [Sales] ELSE 0 END; then the aggregate SUM(...) / SUM([Sales]).

Check what you just learned

1. Which is an aggregate calculation?
  • [Sales] - [Profit]
  • SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) (correct)
  • IF [Profit] < 0 THEN "Loss" END
  • UPPER([Region])

It aggregates before dividing.

2. SUM([Profit]) / [Sales] fails because:
  • Tableau cannot divide
  • Profit is a dimension
  • It mixes aggregate and non-aggregate values (correct)
  • It is too long

A total cannot be divided by a single row.
keyPoints: Row-level calculations run per row; aggregate calculations run per mark.
Calculate ratios as SUM / SUM, not an average of ratios.
You cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate values.

topics.title: Table calculations: running totals, percent of total, rank
topics.html:
A table calculation works on the values already in the view, across the marks, after the data has been aggregated. Running totals, percent of total, rank and differences are table calculations. In Tableau you add the common ones with Quick Table Calculation on a pill's menu.

Common quick table calculations
CalculationWhat it doesExample
Running TotalAdds each mark to those before itCumulative sales through the year
Percent of TotalEach mark as a share of all marksEach category's share of sales
Rank1 for the largest, 2 for the next, and so onCustomers ranked by profit
DifferenceThis mark minus the previous oneMonth-on-month change
Percent DifferenceThe change as a share of the previous markMonth-on-month growth %
Moving AverageThe average of the last few marksA smoothed trend

A running total

The line shows each month's sales. Open the menu on the Sales pill and choose Running total, then Percent of total, Rank and Difference, and see how the numbers change.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

Direction matters

A running total of sales by month, split by Region.

  1. The calculation runs along the months, separately for each region (the partition).
  2. Each region gets its own running total.
  3. If it ran across regions instead, you would add the regions together within each month, which is rarely wanted.

Answer. Every table calculation has a direction (what it moves along) and a partition (what it restarts for). Check both.

Watch out

Table calculations depend on the layout of the view. Add or remove a dimension and the calculation can change meaning or break. If you need a figure that does not depend on the layout, use a level-of-detail expression (next lessons).

Common mistakes

  • A running total that restarts or runs across the wrong dimension.
  • Filtering out the first mark and wondering why the difference calculation is blank.
  • Using a table calculation where a fixed figure was needed.
Try it yourself: Which quick table calculation shows each category's share of total sales?

Model answer. Percent of Total.

Check what you just learned

1. A running total adds:
  • Nothing
  • All marks into one
  • Only the largest
  • Each mark to those before it (correct)

It accumulates along the axis.

2. Table calculations are worked out:
  • After aggregation, across the marks in the view (correct)
  • Before aggregation, per row
  • At the data source
  • Only in dashboards

They use the aggregated marks.
keyPoints: Table calculations work on the aggregated marks in the view.
Running total, percent of total, rank and difference cover most needs.
They depend on the view's layout, direction and partition.

topics.title: Level of detail expressions: FIXED, INCLUDE and EXCLUDE
topics.html:
Normally Tableau calculates at the level of detail of the view: the dimensions on the shelves decide how the rows are grouped. A level of detail (LOD) expression lets you calculate at a different level, so a figure does not change when the view does.

The three LOD expressions
ExpressionCalculates atExample
{ FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales]) }Exactly the dimensions you name, whatever is in the viewEach region's total, even in a chart split by category
{ INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales]) }The view's level plus the dimensions you addEach customer's total, then averaged per region: AVG({ INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales]) })
{ EXCLUDE [Category] : SUM([Sales]) }The view's level minus the dimensions you removeThe region total while the view shows categories
Formula · Share within a group, with FIXED

Region Sales = { FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales]) } Share of Region = SUM([Sales]) / MAX([Region Sales])

The FIXED field is each region's total on every row; dividing each mark's sales by it gives the share of its region.

Share of region with a FIXED expression

Create the two fields from the formula box above (one per line, one at a time). Put Region on Columns, Share of Region on Rows and Category on Color: each region's stack adds up to 100%.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Worked example

INCLUDE: the average customer

'What does the average customer spend, by region?' The view has only Region on it.

  1. SUM([Sales]) per region is the region total: not what is asked.
  2. AVG({ INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales]) }) first totals sales per customer within each region, then averages those totals.
  3. The answer is the average customer's spend in each region.

Answer. INCLUDE adds a level of detail inside the view, then aggregates it back up.

Watch out

FIXED expressions run before dimension filters (but after context filters). A FIXED calculation will not change when you filter a normal dimension, which is often wanted (a region's total stays the same) and sometimes a surprise. Add the filter to context if the calculation should respect it.

Common mistakes

  • Using a table calculation where a FIXED expression was needed.
  • Forgetting that INCLUDE and EXCLUDE need an outer aggregate.
  • Expecting a FIXED expression to respond to an ordinary filter.
Try it yourself: Which LOD would give each customer's total sales regardless of the view?

Model answer. { FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales]) }

Check what you just learned

1. A FIXED expression calculates:
  • At the view's level
  • At exactly the named dimensions whatever the view (correct)
  • Only for dates
  • After table calculations

It fixes the level of detail.

2. INCLUDE [Customer] makes the level of detail:
  • The view's level minus Customer
  • Only Customer
  • The view's level plus Customer (correct)
  • The whole table

It adds a dimension.
keyPoints: FIXED calculates at the named level whatever the view; INCLUDE adds dimensions; EXCLUDE removes them.
LOD expressions do not depend on the view's layout, unlike table calculations.
FIXED runs before ordinary dimension filters.

topics.title: Choosing between calculation types
topics.html:
Four tools, one decision: how do you choose?

Which calculation?
You needUse
A per-row value or flag (profit minus cost, a band)Row-level calculated field
A ratio or aggregate that follows the view (profit ratio)Aggregate calculated field
A value that depends on the order or position of marks (running total, rank, difference)Table calculation
A figure at a different level than the view (customer total, region total)LOD expression
Worked example

The same question three ways

What share of its region's sales is each category?

  1. Table calculation: Percent of Total, computed within each region (works, but depends on the layout).
  2. FIXED LOD: SUM([Sales]) / MAX({ FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales]) }) (works whatever the layout).
  3. Both give the same numbers here; the LOD survives a change in the view.

Answer. Prefer the LOD when you need the figure to stay stable as the view changes; use a table calculation for quick, layout-based questions.

Habits for calculations

  • Name fields clearly (Profit Ratio, not Calculation1).
  • Comment complex formulas with //.
  • Build big calculations from small ones.
  • Test a calculation on a few rows you can check by hand.
  • Watch performance: LODs and table calculations on very large data can be slow.
Watch out

A calculation that gives a number is not a calculation that gives the right number. Check one case by hand against the data (or a text table of the underlying values).

Common mistakes

  • Writing a long calculation without testing parts.
  • Choosing a table calculation when the view will change.
  • Calculating a ratio from rounded numbers.

Check what you just learned

1. A running total is best done with:
  • A row-level field
  • A filter
  • A FIXED LOD
  • A table calculation (correct)

It depends on the order of marks.

2. A customer's total that must not change with the view uses:
  • A FIXED LOD expression (correct)
  • A table calculation
  • A pie
  • Nothing

FIXED fixes the level.

Key terms: flip and sort

Calculated field
A new field defined by a formula.
Row-level
Worked out for each row.
Aggregate
Worked out per mark.
Table calculation
Works across the marks of the view.
LOD expression
Calculates at a chosen level of detail.
FIXED
Calculates at exactly the named dimensions.
Partition
What a table calculation restarts for.
keyPoints: Row-level for per-row values, aggregate for view-following ratios, table calculations for position-based figures, LOD for a different level.
Test calculations by hand on a few rows.
Name and comment them.

modules.title: Design, dashboards and storytelling
modules.summary: Use visual encoding well, design dashboards people can read in seconds, make them interactive with actions, and tell a story with data.
modules.outcome: You can choose encodings by how accurately people read them, lay out a dashboard, use filter and highlight actions, make a view accessible, and structure a story.
modules.intro: A chart can be correct and still fail: too much colour, a pie with twelve slices, an axis that exaggerates, a dashboard with so much on it that nobody knows where to look. Design is how you make the right answer easy to see. This module teaches the research-backed principles (what the eye reads accurately), how to arrange and connect views into a dashboard, and how to turn a dashboard into a story with a point. Tableau Desktop and Tableau Public are desktop applications and do not run in a browser tab, so the steps described here (opening Tableau, connecting, publishing) are explained rather than run. What does run here is a practice viz builder with the same ideas: fields on the Columns and Rows shelves, the Marks card, filters, calculated fields and table calculations, on a real table.

topics.title: Visual encoding: what the eye reads well
topics.html:
Every chart turns numbers into visual properties: position, length, angle, area, colour. Researchers (notably Cleveland and McGill) have ranked how accurately people judge each, and the ranking should shape your choices.

From most to least accurate
EncodingAccuracyExample
Position on a common scaleMost accurateDots on the same axis, a bar's end
LengthVery goodBars from a shared baseline
Angle and slopeFairPie slices, a line's steepness
AreaWeakBubble size, treemap boxes
Colour intensity (saturation)WeakA heat map's shades
Colour hueGood for telling categories apart, poor for quantitiesDifferent colours for different regions

So: put the most important comparison on position or length (a bar chart or a dot plot), and use colour to separate categories or highlight, not to carry the main numbers. That is why a sorted bar chart beats a pie for comparison, and why a heat map is for spotting patterns, not reading values.

The same data, two encodings

Sales by category as bars (length: easy to compare). Switch the mark to Pie (angle: harder). Which makes the order obvious?

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Order ID, Order Date, Region, Category, Sub-Category, Segment, Customer, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

Using colour well

  • Use one accent colour to highlight what matters and grey for the rest.
  • Use a sequential palette (light to dark) for a measure and a categorical palette for categories.
  • Use a diverging palette (two hues around a neutral midpoint) when there is a meaningful centre such as zero profit.
  • Keep colour meaning consistent across a dashboard.
  • Design for colour-blind readers: avoid red and green as the only signal; add labels or shapes.
Watch out

Colour is the most over-used encoding. A chart with eight colours has no emphasis: everything shouts. Ask what you want the reader to notice, and colour only that.

Common mistakes

  • Encoding the key comparison with area or colour intensity.
  • Rainbow palettes for ordered numbers.
  • Red and green as the only difference.
Try it yourself: Which is easier to compare: five bars or five pie slices of the same values?

Model answer. The bars: length from a common baseline is judged more accurately than angle.

Check what you just learned

1. Which encoding is read most accurately?
  • Colour intensity
  • Position on a common scale (correct)
  • Area
  • Angle

Position beats the others.

2. Colour hue is best used to:
  • Show exact quantities
  • Replace axes
  • Tell categories apart or highlight (correct)
  • Decorate

Hue separates categories.
keyPoints: Position and length are read most accurately; angle, area and colour intensity least.
Put the key comparison on position or length; use colour to separate or highlight.
Use sequential, categorical and diverging palettes appropriately, and design for colour blindness.

topics.title: Dashboards: layout and actions
topics.html:
A dashboard brings several sheets together so a reader can see the situation and explore it. Two things make or break it: layout and interactivity.

Layout principles

  • Start with the question and the reader. A dashboard for executives answers 'are we on track?'; one for analysts supports exploration.
  • Put the most important view top left, and give it the most space.
  • Group related views, align them to a grid and keep spacing even.
  • Use containers (horizontal and vertical layout containers) so the layout stays tidy when the window resizes.
  • Limit the number of views: three to five is plenty.
  • Set a fixed or automatic size on purpose, and add device layouts for phones and tablets.
Dashboard actions
ActionWhat it doesUse for
FilterSelecting marks in one sheet filters other sheetsClick a region, and every other view shows only that region
HighlightSelecting marks highlights related marks in other sheetsSee where one category sits across charts
Go to sheet / URLJump to another sheet or open a web pageNavigation and drill to detail
Change parameter / setSelecting a mark changes a parameter or setAdvanced interactive designs
Worked example

A sales dashboard for managers

Managers want to know whether sales are on track and where to look.

  1. Top left: a monthly sales line against target.
  2. Right: a sorted bar chart of profit by sub-category, with loss-makers in a different colour.
  3. Below: a heat map of region by category.
  4. A filter action: clicking a region filters all three views.

Answer. In five seconds the manager sees the trend; one click answers 'is it the same in the West?'

Watch out

A dashboard is not a place to show everything you built. Every extra chart competes for attention. If a view does not help answer the question, remove it.

Common mistakes

  • Ten views on one dashboard.
  • Filters with no indication of what is filtered.
  • A layout that breaks on a laptop screen or a phone.
Try it yourself: What does a filter action do?

Model answer. Selecting marks in one sheet filters the data in the other sheets on the dashboard.

Check what you just learned

1. How many views suit a typical dashboard?
  • None
  • Twenty
  • One hundred
  • About three to five (correct)

Fewer views read faster.

2. A filter action means:
  • Selecting marks in one sheet filters the others (correct)
  • Filters are hidden
  • A colour change
  • A new data source

Clicking marks filters other sheets.
keyPoints: Start from the question and reader; key view top left; three to five views.
Use containers for a tidy, resizable layout; add device layouts.
Actions (filter, highlight, go to) make a dashboard explorable.

topics.title: Accessibility, honesty and polish
topics.html:
The finishing touches decide whether a dashboard is trusted and usable.

Accessibility

  • Colour contrast between text and background must be strong.
  • Not colour alone: add labels, shapes or patterns so colour-blind readers can tell marks apart.
  • Alt text on dashboards and key views, so screen readers can describe them.
  • Readable font sizes and a logical reading order.
  • Titles that say something, not just the field names.

Honest charts

  • Bars start at zero; do not truncate the axis.
  • Label axes and units; include the time period and filters in the title or caption.
  • Do not use a dual axis to make two unrelated lines look correlated.
  • Avoid 3D and decoration that distorts values.
  • Show uncertainty where it exists.
Polish checklist
CheckQuestion
TitleDoes it state the finding or the question?
LabelsAre axes, units and the key marks labelled?
TooltipsDo they add useful context, not a data dump?
ColourOne accent, consistent meaning, colour-blind safe?
ClutterCan any gridline, border or legend be removed?
DefaultsIs the default view the one most readers need?
Worked example

Fixing a misleading dual axis

A chart overlays sales and temperature with two separate vertical axes, scaled so the lines track each other.

  1. The relationship looks strong, but it was created by choosing the axis scales.
  2. Change to two small charts stacked on a shared time axis, each starting at its natural baseline.
  3. Now any real relationship is visible without the scaling trick.

Answer. If you can make two lines look correlated just by changing the axes, the chart is not telling you anything.

Watch out

A dashboard that looks professional but is wrong is worse than a plain one that is right. Reconcile key numbers to a trusted source before publishing.

Common mistakes

  • Low-contrast grey text on a grey background.
  • A truncated axis to exaggerate a change.
  • Tooltips full of every field in the data.

Check what you just learned

1. To help colour-blind readers you should:
  • Use red and green only
  • Add labels or shapes as well as colour (correct)
  • Use more colours
  • Remove the legend

Do not rely on colour alone.

2. A truncated bar chart axis:
  • Is honest
  • Is required
  • Exaggerates differences (correct)
  • Improves accuracy

Bar length must be proportional.
keyPoints: Accessibility: contrast, not colour alone, alt text, readable text, meaningful titles.
Honest charts: zero baselines, labelled axes, no misleading dual axes.
Polish by checking title, labels, tooltips, colour and clutter, and reconcile numbers.

topics.title: Telling a story with data
topics.html:
A story in Tableau is a sequence of sheets or dashboards (story points), each with a caption, that guides a reader to a conclusion. The tool matters less than the shape of the narrative.

Worked example

A four-point story

Why did profit fall in 2025 despite higher sales?

  1. Point 1: Sales rose a little in 2025 (a line chart).
  2. Point 2: Profit fell (a second line: the gap is the surprise).
  3. Point 3: Furniture lost money overall, driven by Tables and Bookcases (a scatter with the loss-makers highlighted).
  4. Point 4: Recommendation: review the pricing and costs of Tables and Bookcases before the next promotion (a short text caption).

Answer. Each point adds one idea, and the headline of each caption says it in a sentence.

Habits of good data storytellers

  • Headline first: caption each view with what to notice, not what it is.
  • One idea per view.
  • Guide the eye: highlight the one mark that matters, and grey the rest.
  • Show the evidence, then the conclusion, then the action.
  • Know your audience: an executive wants the answer; an analyst wants the method too.
Watch out

Do not hide what does not fit your story. If other explanations exist, say so; it builds trust and protects you from being wrong in public.

Common mistakes

  • A story that is a slideshow of charts with no point.
  • Captions that only name the chart.
  • A conclusion the data does not support.
Try it yourself: Write a headline caption for a chart showing profit falling while sales rise.

Model answer. For example: 'Sales rose slightly in 2025, but profit fell: we are selling more of the products that lose money.'

Check what you just learned

1. A good story caption:
  • Names the chart
  • Repeats the axis
  • Is blank
  • States what to notice (correct)

Headline first.

2. A data story ends with:
  • A clear action or conclusion (correct)
  • The raw data
  • More charts
  • A colour legend

Readers need to know what to do.

Key terms: flip and sort

Encoding
How data is shown: position, length, angle, area, colour.
Dashboard
Several sheets on one page with interactivity.
Container
A layout object that keeps a dashboard tidy.
Action
Clicking marks filters, highlights or navigates.
Device layout
A layout for phones or tablets.
Story point
One step in a Tableau story.
Diverging palette
Two hues around a neutral midpoint.
keyPoints: A story has context, a surprise, an explanation and an action.
Caption each view with the point, one idea per view.
Be honest about what the data does and does not show.

modules.title: Connecting, preparing and speeding up data
modules.summary: Choose between live connections and extracts, combine tables with joins, unions, relationships and blends, reshape data, and keep dashboards fast.
modules.outcome: You can choose live or extract, pick the right way to combine tables, reshape data with pivot, and apply the main performance habits.
modules.intro: The quality of a Tableau dashboard is limited by its data. This module covers how Tableau connects to data, how tables are combined, how to prepare and reshape data (in Tableau and in Tableau Prep), and the habits that keep dashboards fast. These are desktop features, so they are explained with scenarios and checked with sorting activities. The ideas match the SQL and Power Query ideas you may already know.

topics.title: Live connections and extracts
topics.html:
When you connect Tableau to data you choose how it reads it.

Live or extract?
Live connectionExtract (.hyper)
How it worksEach view queries the source when it is drawnA fast, compressed snapshot of the data is stored with the workbook or on the server
Data freshnessAlways currentAs current as the last refresh
SpeedAs fast as the sourceUsually much faster
Offline useNoYes
Good forFast databases, real-time needsSlow sources, large files, shared dashboards, offline work
Worked example

Choosing for a monthly report

A dashboard reads a slow, shared database and is refreshed monthly.

  1. A live connection would hit the database on every click, slowly, for every viewer.
  2. An extract refreshed overnight serves everyone from a fast snapshot.
  3. The data is current enough for a monthly report.

Answer. Use an extract unless you truly need up-to-the-minute data.

Extract habits

  • Filter the extract to the rows and columns the dashboard needs (extract filters), so it stays small.
  • Aggregate to the level the dashboard needs, if possible.
  • Schedule refreshes on the server after the source updates.
  • Use incremental refresh for large tables where new rows are added.
Watch out

An extract is a copy. If the source changes and the extract is not refreshed, the dashboard quietly shows old numbers. Show the last refresh date on the dashboard.

Common mistakes

  • Live connections to a slow database for a dashboard with many viewers.
  • An extract of every column of a huge table.
  • Forgetting to refresh.
Try it yourself: When is a live connection the better choice?

Model answer. When data must be current to the moment and the source is fast enough to answer each query.

Check what you just learned

1. An extract is:
  • A live query
  • A fast stored snapshot of the data (correct)
  • A chart
  • A filter

It is a compressed copy.

2. A risk of extracts is:
  • They are always slow
  • They cannot be filtered
  • They can be out of date if not refreshed (correct)
  • They need a gateway

Refresh them.
keyPoints: Live queries the source each time; an extract is a fast stored snapshot.
Use extracts for slow sources and shared dashboards; filter and aggregate them.
Refresh on a schedule and show the last refresh.

topics.title: Combining tables: joins, unions, relationships and blends
topics.html:
Real analysis usually needs more than one table. Tableau offers several ways to combine them.

Ways to combine data
MethodWhat it doesUse when
RelationshipKeeps tables separate and joins them as needed for each view, at the right level of detailThe default in Tableau's data model: the safest way to link tables
JoinCombines tables row by row into one (inner, left, right, full outer)You want one flat table and understand the key
UnionStacks tables with the same columns on top of each otherMonthly files with the same layout
Data blendCombines separate data sources at the level of the view, on shared dimensionsTables from different sources that cannot be joined
Cross-database joinJoins tables from different databasesOccasional, small-scale combining

Relationships are usually the best start: Tableau joins the tables for each view, using only the tables the view needs, and keeps the right level of detail, so totals are not inflated the way a careless join can inflate them. A join fixes the combination in advance, so a one-to-many join can repeat the 'one' side's values (the fan-out problem from the SQL course).

Worked example

Why a join inflated a total

Orders (one row per order) are joined to payments (two payments for some orders).

  1. Orders with two payments appear twice.
  2. SUM of an order-level amount counts those orders twice.
  3. A relationship, or aggregating payments to one row per order before joining, avoids the double count.

Answer. Always check row counts and totals after combining tables.

Preparing data

  • Pivot columns to rows (wide to long) so each fact is one row: Tableau's Pivot, or Tableau Prep.
  • Split columns, fix data types and rename fields in the data source pane.
  • Clean with the Data Interpreter for messy spreadsheets, or Tableau Prep for repeatable flows.
  • Hide unused fields and group them into folders.
  • Document calculations and sources.
Watch out

Dimensions with the same name in two tables are not automatically the same. Check keys for type mismatches and stray spaces before relating or joining.

Common mistakes

  • Joining on a column that is not unique and not noticing the extra rows.
  • Using a blend when a relationship would do.
  • Leaving data in wide format (a column per month) and fighting it in every view.
Try it yourself: Which method stacks twelve monthly files with the same columns?

Model answer. A union.

Check what you just learned

1. Which combines monthly files with the same columns?
  • Join
  • Filter
  • Blend
  • Union (correct)

A union stacks them.

2. Relationships are useful because they:
  • Join tables per view at the right level of detail (correct)
  • Always copy data
  • Need no keys
  • Remove filters

They avoid accidental fan-outs.
keyPoints: Relationships keep tables separate and join per view; joins combine rows; unions stack; blends link sources by shared dimensions.
Check row counts and totals after combining tables.
Pivot wide data to long, and clean before analysis.

topics.title: Performance: keeping dashboards fast
topics.html:
A slow dashboard is a dashboard nobody uses. Most of the time the cause is one of a few things, and Tableau can tell you which.

Common causes and fixes
CauseFix
Too many marks (hundreds of thousands of points)Aggregate, filter, or use fewer detail dimensions
Too many views and filters on one dashboardFewer views; use fewer quick filters; apply 'Apply' buttons to filters
A live connection to a slow sourceUse an extract; filter and aggregate it
Complex calculations on large data (string functions, nested LODs, many table calculations)Simplify; pre-calculate in the data source or in Tableau Prep
Custom SQL that scans everything for every queryUse tables or views; add indexes at the source
Large, high-resolution images and many sheetsCompress images; remove unused sheets
Worked example

Reading a slow dashboard

A dashboard takes 25 seconds to load.

  1. Performance Recording shows one scatter sheet rendering 400,000 marks.
  2. The reader only needs one dot per customer, not per order line: aggregate.
  3. Marks drop to 3,000; load time drops to 4 seconds.

Answer. Measure first, then fix the biggest thing.

Habits that keep dashboards fast

  • Show an overview first, with detail on demand (drill-through, tooltips).
  • Prefer extracts for shared dashboards.
  • Keep calculations simple, or move them upstream.
  • Use context filters sparingly; they create a temporary table.
  • Test on the slowest realistic device.
Watch out

Do not optimise by guessing. Use Performance Recording (Help → Settings and Performance) to see what the time is spent on, and fix that.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a filter to every field.
  • Plotting every row when a summary would do.
  • Never measuring.
Try it yourself: Name two ways to reduce marks in a view.

Model answer. Aggregate to a coarser level, and filter to the data needed (or use fewer detail dimensions).

Check what you just learned

1. The first step in speeding up a dashboard is to:
  • Guess
  • Measure with Performance Recording (correct)
  • Add filters
  • Add colour

Find the real cause.

2. Reducing the number of marks helps because:
  • It prints faster
  • It adds colour
  • Tableau draws fewer shapes and queries less data (correct)
  • It sorts

Fewer marks mean less work.

Key terms: flip and sort

Live connection
Queries the source each time.
Extract
A stored, fast snapshot of the data.
Relationship
A flexible link between tables, joined per view.
Join
Combines tables row by row.
Union
Stacks tables with the same columns.
Blend
Links separate sources by shared dimensions.
Performance Recording
A tool that shows where time is spent.
keyPoints: Too many marks, views, filters and heavy calculations are the usual causes of slowness.
Use extracts, simple calculations and fewer quick filters.
Measure with Performance Recording, then fix the biggest cause.

Where to publish
DestinationAudienceNotes
Tableau PublicAnyone on the internetFree; everything is public. Never for private data
Tableau CloudYour organisation, in a hosted serviceManaged by Tableau; sign-in and permissions apply
Tableau ServerYour organisation, on your own serversYou manage the infrastructure
A packaged workbook (.twbx)A person you send it toContains the data: share carefully

Server building blocks

  • Projects organise content into folders, and permissions can be set per project.
  • Workbooks hold sheets and dashboards; published data sources are shared, governed connections to data.
  • Permissions control who can view, edit, download, delete or administer content.
  • Subscriptions and alerts email a snapshot of a view on a schedule or when a value crosses a threshold.
  • Refresh schedules update extracts on a timetable.
Worked example

Publishing a data source once

Five analysts each connect to the sales database and write the same calculations.

  1. Instead, an owner publishes one data source with the agreed calculations and an extract refreshed nightly.
  2. Analysts connect to it from Desktop and build workbooks.
  3. A fix to a calculation is made once and reaches every workbook.

Answer. Shared data sources give one definition of each metric.

Watch out

Embedding credentials or sharing a workbook that contains the data can leak information. Publish data sources with the right authentication and share through the server, not by email.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing company data to Tableau Public.
  • Emailing packaged workbooks that contain sensitive data.
  • Every analyst building their own version of a metric.
Try it yourself: Why publish a shared data source instead of embedding the data in every workbook?

Model answer. One governed definition and refresh serves every workbook, and a fix is made once.

Check what you just learned

1. Tableau Public is suitable for:
  • Confidential data
  • Server administration
  • Row-level security
  • Public data you are happy to share with anyone (correct)

Everything published there is public.

2. A published data source gives you:
  • One governed definition used by many workbooks (correct)
  • A new colour palette
  • Faster typing
  • A filter

Reuse and consistency.
keyPoints: Publish to Cloud or Server for organisations; Public is for public data only.
Projects, permissions, subscriptions and refresh schedules organise and deliver content.
Share data sources, not copies of data.

topics.title: Row-level security and permissions
topics.html:
Permissions control what a person can do with content. Row-level security (RLS) controls which rows of data they see inside it. You often need both.

Two layers of access
LayerControlsExample
PermissionsWho can view, edit or download a workbook or data sourceSales managers can view the Sales project; only analysts can edit
Row-level securityWhich rows of data each viewer seesEach regional manager sees only their region's sales in the same dashboard

One common way to do RLS is a user filter based on the signed-in user. A calculated field compares a column of the data with the user's name or group, and the view is filtered to the rows where it is true:

A user-filter calculation
IdeaCalculation
Match the manager column to the signed-in user[Manager Email] = USERNAME()
Match a groupISMEMBEROF('West Sales')
Use it as a data-source filterAdd the calculated field as a filter that keeps True
Worked example

One dashboard, many views

A sales dashboard is used by four regional managers.

  1. A data source filter keeps rows where the Region's manager is the signed-in user.
  2. Each manager opens the same dashboard and sees only their own region.
  3. Head office sees everything through a group that bypasses the filter.

Answer. RLS replaces four copies of the dashboard with one.

Watch out

Row-level security must be applied at the data source and tested as each kind of user. If a person can edit or download the workbook or connect to the data directly, a filter inside the workbook may not protect them. Apply the filter in a published data source and limit who can edit it.

Common mistakes

  • Hiding a sheet and calling it security.
  • Testing only as the author, who sees everything.
  • Relying on a filter that a user with edit rights can remove.
Try it yourself: Write a user-filter calculation that keeps rows where the Manager Email column matches the signed-in user.

Model answer. [Manager Email] = USERNAME()

Check what you just learned

1. Row-level security controls:
  • Colours
  • Which rows each viewer sees (correct)
  • Fonts
  • Chart types

It filters the data per user.

2. USERNAME() returns:
  • The server
  • The workbook name
  • The signed-in user's name (correct)
  • A colour

It identifies the viewer.
keyPoints: Permissions control actions; row-level security controls which rows a user sees.
A user filter compares data with USERNAME() or group membership.
Apply RLS in a published data source and test as each user type.

topics.title: Governance and analytics features
topics.html:
Governance is how an organisation keeps its analytics trusted, consistent and secure as more people create content.

Governance practices

  • Certified data sources that the data team vouches for, so people use them instead of making copies.
  • Naming standards and clear descriptions for data sources and calculations.
  • A defined content lifecycle: draft, test, publish, review and retire.
  • Clear ownership for each data source and dashboard.
  • Least privilege: give the lowest access that lets people do their work.
  • Usage monitoring: remove dashboards nobody opens.

Tableau also has built-in analytics features you can add to a view from the Analytics pane. They are quick, but use them with care.

Analytics pane features
FeatureWhat it doesCaution
Trend lineFits a line or curve through the marksShows a pattern, not a cause; check the fit (R-squared)
ForecastProjects a time series forward with a statistical modelNeeds enough history; show the uncertainty band; it is not a promise
ClustersGroups similar marks with k-meansGroups depend on the fields and the number of clusters you choose
Reference lineDraws an average, median, target or constantState what the line is
Box plot / distribution bandShows the spread of a measureUseful for outliers
Worked example

A forecast with honesty

A forecast line extends monthly sales three months ahead.

  1. The shaded band shows the range of likely values, not just one line.
  2. The caption says: 'Forecast assumes the 2025 pattern continues; it does not include planned price changes.'
  3. The decision-maker plans for the range.

Answer. A forecast is a range with assumptions, never a promise.

Watch out

Built-in analytics make it easy to produce an impressive-looking forecast from too little data. Always check the history length, show the uncertainty and state the assumptions.

Common mistakes

  • Uncertified, duplicated data sources with different numbers.
  • A forecast presented as a certainty.
  • A trend line read as proof of cause.

Check what you just learned

1. A certified data source is:
  • Any file
  • A filter
  • A colour
  • One the data team vouches for as trusted (correct)

It is the preferred source.

2. A forecast should be shown with:
  • A range and stated assumptions (correct)
  • Only a line
  • No caption
  • Fewer data

Uncertainty must be visible.

Key terms: flip and sort

Project
A folder of server content with permissions.
Published data source
A shared, governed connection.
Permission
What a person may do with content.
Row-level security
Which rows each viewer sees.
USERNAME()
The signed-in user's name.
Certified data source
A source the data team vouches for.
Forecast
A projection with uncertainty.
keyPoints: Governance: certified data sources, naming, ownership, lifecycle, least privilege, usage monitoring.
Trend lines, forecasts, clusters and reference lines are quick analytics.
Show uncertainty and assumptions; a trend is not a cause.

capstone.summary: Build the view that shows which sub-categories sell a lot but lose money, write the dashboard brief and findings, and pass the final assessment.
capstone.intro: You can now build the core charts, write calculated fields, table calculations and level-of-detail expressions, design for the reader, and describe how data is prepared, speeded up, published and secured. In this final project you play the analyst for Kiran Office Supplies. First, in the viz builder, build the scatter that answers the management question: which sub-categories sell a lot but lose money? Then, in the document lab, write the dashboard brief: the finding, the views, who sees what, a limit of the data and your recommendation. Finally take the assessment, which covers the whole course.
